newsitem.title: USA: Electric deregulation poses risks for US producers.
newsitem.headline: Electric deregulation poses risks for US producers.

text.p: Deregulation of the U.S. electric industry could trim the growth of natural gas consumption by electric generators in the coming years, an industry consulting firm said Thursday.
"Electric deregulation represents more of a risk than an opportunity for natural gas," said Robert Baron, senior project manager at ICF Kaiser International Inc.

If generators come to rely on baseload coal plants to produce electricity, gas consumption by the industry would remain relatively steady, rising to 3.5 trillion cubic feet (tcf) a year by 2010 from 3.3 tcf in 1995, the firm said.

Gas demand for electric generation had been projected to rise to nearly 6 tcf a year if the industry was not deregulated, and a shift to use of smaller gas-fired plants in the wake of deregulation could still boost demand to 6.2 tcf a year by 2010, the Fairfax, Va.-based firm said.

Deregulation of the electric industry is widely expected to boost reliance on relatively low-cost gas-fired plants, although some analysts predict lower gas demand as the industry finds more economical ways to wheel excess electric power generated by baseload coal plants.

"The point we were trying to make in the study is that there are a set of circumstance where that (gas) demand increase will not be as large as certain people are anticipating," Michael Godec, an ICF vice president, said.

On the supply side of the equation, more stringent environmental regulations are expected to boost exploration costs and trim production by U.S. natural gas producers in the coming years, the firm said.
Environmental compliance will add an estimated $3 billion a year to the industry's costs and could trim domestic production by about 1.7 tcf a year, the firm estimated.

While environmental compliance inflates drilling budgets and threatens to trim production, some of the higher expenses should be offset by new technologies steadily cutting exploration and production costs, it said.

Aggressive use of three-dimensional seismic surveys, satellite data and improved drilling techniques, among other things, could generate 21 tcf of new reserves and 1.3 tcf a year in additional production for North American producers, the firm said.
The savings could translate into a 15 cent per million cubic feet reduction in citygate prices, the firm said.
